title: Training audit trace (seeds thin, mean bold): is the result real or seed noise?
summary: A single training run can look like progress that is only luck. This audit trace draws every random seed as a thin line, the mean as a bold line and a noise floor, so you can see whether an improvement is larger than the run-to-run noise.

media.alt: Semi-log plot of validation loss against epoch: eight thin blue seed curves, a bold teal mean curve falling from 1 to about 0.055, a dashed amber horizontal noise-floor line at about 0.068 with a shaded band below it.
media.caption: Reference render of class F6.5 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Is the result real or seed noise?
read_the_figure.axes: x: epoch (0 to 200), linear. y: validation loss, logarithmic (about 0.04 to 1.1).
look_at: How wide is the spread of the seeds at the start and at the end?
Where does the mean enter the noise band, and when do all seeds sit inside it?
Are all seeds drawn, so no run is hidden?
How is the noise floor defined (here, the seed spread of the baseline)?
as_drawn: Eight seeds (thin blue) and their mean (bold teal) fall from about 1 at epoch 1 to about 0.057 at epoch 200 (the seeds end between about 0.052 and 0.067).
The dashed amber floor is at about 0.0675, a shaded band below it extends to 0.04. The mean crosses the floor at about epoch 157, and all eight seeds are below it from about epoch 179.
At epoch 100 the seeds spread from about 0.10 to 0.17 around a mean of about 0.13, a factor of about 1.8.
The legend states the seed count (n = 8) and defines the floor as the seed spread of the baseline.
read_the_figure.proves: If a claimed improvement lies above the noise floor, defined as the seed spread of the baseline, it is unlikely to be luck. If the mean merely enters the band, the plot shows no distinguishable progress there.
if_wrong: Only the mean drawn: the reader cannot judge the spread, so a lucky seed can pass for a trend.
No floor: the reader has no standard by which to call a gap real.
Few seeds (n = 2 or 3): the spread itself is poorly known; do not trust the band.
must_check: all seeds drawn: the individual runs are the evidence, and hiding them hides the noise.
noise floor: it is the standard against which a difference is judged, and it should be defined in the legend.

terms.meaning: The integer that initialises the random number generator; different seeds give different initial weights and data order.
The loss on held-out data, used to judge generalisation.
The size of run-to-run variation of a baseline method; differences smaller than this are not distinguishable from luck.
The spread of the seed mean: the seed standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of seeds.
One pass over the training data.

remember: SE of a mean = s / sqrt(n).
SE of a difference of two means with n seeds each = s sqrt(2/n).
A difference is convincing when it exceeds about 2 SE of the difference.
For n = 8 this is about one seed standard deviation.
Draw every seed and state the floor.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position on x is the epoch and on y the validation loss on a log scale. Each thin blue line is one seed, so there are eight of them; the bold teal line is the mean of the eight; the dashed amber line is the noise floor and the shading below it is the band of results that cannot be told apart from the baseline. Line weight encodes importance: the evidence is thin, the summary is bold.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: if you ran the same experiment eight times and got eight different curves, a single curve cannot tell you whether a small improvement is real. Drawing all of them shows how much they wander, and the floor gives a yardstick. A mean that crosses the yardstick but is lost among the seeds is not progress. The log axis keeps the early steep part and the late flat part readable.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: The floor here comes from the baseline spread and is a threshold on single runs: for comparing means of several seeds the right yardstick is smaller (a factor of 1 / sqrt(n) for each mean). With only eight seeds the spread itself is uncertain. A log axis makes noise at low loss look smaller than the same relative noise at high loss. And seeds control only some sources of randomness: data splits and hyper-parameters are fixed.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A table of the final mean and standard deviation per method, with a statistical test between methods, is more precise. Violin or dot plots of the final loss per seed show the distribution. A paired plot (same seed, two methods) removes seed effects when the seeds are shared.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add the 95 percent interval of the mean as a ribbon, mark the epoch at which every seed has entered the noise band, and draw the baseline method's seeds in grey behind.

steps.title: Spread of a mean
steps.note: With n = 8 seeds the mean is known to about s / 2.8.

steps.title: Comparing two methods
steps.note: For n = 8 the threshold 2 SE is about one seed standard deviation, s. Verified numerically (factor 0.5 and 1.0).

steps.title: Noise on a log axis
steps.tex: \ln L_i=\ln\bar L+\varepsilon_i\;\Rightarrow\;\text{seed spread is a ratio, }e^{\pm s_{\ln}}
steps.note: A constant relative noise is a constant vertical spread on a log axis, as at epochs 20 and 100 in the render.

worked.title: Reading the audit from the reference render
worked.problem: (1) At which epoch does the mean enter the noise band? (2) How big is the spread of the seeds at epoch 100? (3) What is the smallest difference between two eight-seed means that is convincing if the seed standard deviation is s?

solution.text: (1) Follow the bold line down to the dashed line: it crosses near epoch 157, and by about epoch 179 every thin line is below it.
(2) At epoch 100 the seeds run from about 0.10 to 0.17 around a mean of 0.13.
(3) Use the standard error of a difference with n = 8.

worked.answer: Epoch 157 (all seeds by about 179); a spread of about a factor 1.8 across seeds at epoch 100; for eight seeds per method a difference of about one seed standard deviation is borderline convincing.

analyze.q: After epoch 180 the mean is in the band and all seeds are below the floor. What would you conclude about further training?
Why does the spread of the seeds look larger around epoch 100 than at the start?
analyze.hint: Different initial rates on a log axis.

analyze.q: What would you change if only two seeds were run?
analyze.hint: How well is a spread known from two numbers?

evaluate.q: A new method's mean lies just below the dashed floor at the end of training. Do you report it as better?
evaluate.hint: Compare means with the right yardstick and consider more seeds.

create: Redraw with the mean's 95 percent ribbon and a vertical line at the epoch where all seeds are inside the band.
Add the baseline's eight seeds in light grey and the new method's in colour on the same axes.

checks.q: Why draw every seed instead of only the mean?
checks.answer: Because the spread between seeds is the noise level; the mean alone cannot show whether a difference is larger than that.

checks.q: Seed standard deviation 0.01, eight seeds per method. What is the standard error of the difference of the means?
checks.answer: 0.01 x sqrt(0.25) = 0.005; a difference above about 0.01 is convincing.

checks.q: The mean of the new method is 5 percent below the baseline mean at the end, and all seeds overlap. How do you decide whether to publish this?
checks.hint: More seeds and the right test.
checks.answer: Increase the number of seeds, compare means with their standard error (or a paired test), and report the interval; with overlapping seeds a 5 percent gap may be within the noise.
